title: Conflict Resolver
learning_objectives: Find solutions that address root causes

events.description: Scenario: You and a classmate were paired on a project. You did 80% of the work, they did 20%. Now they want equal credit. You're frustrated. Before you react, consider their perspective — they mentioned their parent was sick last week. How do you approach this?

choices.label: Start by acknowledging their situation, then discuss the work gap
choices.effect: Leading with empathy opens the conversation. They explain they were at the hospital most nights. Now you can solve the real problem together.

choices.label: Present the work split factually — 'I noticed I did sections 1-4, you did part of 5'
choices.effect: Factual framing avoids blame. 'I noticed' is different from 'you didn't.' They agree and offer to do extra for the next phase.

choices.label: Ask the teacher to mediate before it becomes an argument
choices.effect: Third-party mediation! The teacher helps you both share perspectives without it getting personal.

events.description: The conversation gets emotional. Your classmate says 'You don't understand what I've been going through!' You feel your own frustration rising. What do you do in this moment?

choices.label: Pause — 'You're right, I don't fully understand. Can you tell me?'
choices.effect: De-escalation through validation! When someone feels heard, the emotional temperature drops. They open up about their situation.

choices.label: Use I-statements: 'I feel frustrated because I put in a lot of work'
choices.effect: I-statements express your feelings without attacking. 'I feel frustrated' is different from 'You're lazy.' Both feelings are now on the table.

choices.label: Suggest a 10-minute break before continuing
choices.effect: Emotional regulation! Neither of you will solve this well when emotions are high. A break lets both brains switch from reactive to thoughtful.

events.description: You've both calmed down. Now you need a solution. The project is due in 5 days. How do you move forward?

choices.label: Redistribute remaining work so they can catch up on their share
choices.effect: A forward-looking solution! They take on the presentation prep and bibliography — doable in their situation and adds real value.

choices.label: Suggest noting each person's contributions on the project
choices.effect: Transparent credit! You both get credit for the project but each section shows who contributed what. Fair and honest.

choices.label: Give grace this time, but set clear expectations for Part 2
choices.effect: Sometimes people need grace during hard times. You set up a shared task tracker for Part 2 so expectations are crystal clear.

events.description: Reflecting on this conflict: what's the biggest lesson?

choices.label: Both people's feelings were valid — the conflict was the situation, not the people
choices.effect: Key insight! Most conflicts are situational, not personal. Separating the person from the problem is the foundation of conflict resolution.

choices.label: If we'd talked earlier, it wouldn't have built up
choices.effect: Prevention! A quick check-in in Week 1 ('How are you doing on your sections?') catches problems before they become conflicts.

choices.label: There were many possible solutions — not just 'I win, you lose'
choices.effect: Win-win thinking! The best solutions address both people's needs. That's not compromise — it's creative problem-solving.

recap_template: You resolved a real-world conflict using empathy, assertive communication, and creative problem-solving! Conflict resolution isn't about winning — it's about finding solutions that work for everyone.
positive_framing_rules: Never frame either party as the villain
Model de-escalation in all response options
Celebrate emotional regulation as a skill

title: Job Interview Prep

events.description: You have a job interview tomorrow for a part-time position. The interviewer will likely ask: 'Tell me about yourself,' 'Why do you want this job?' and 'What's your biggest strength?' How do you prepare?

choices.label: Write out key points for each question and practice aloud
choices.effect: Preparation builds confidence! You have clear, concise answers ready. Practice out loud makes them feel natural, not scripted.

choices.label: Research the company so you can connect your answers to their values
choices.effect: Impressive! Mentioning specific company details shows genuine interest. 'I saw your community volunteer program and that aligns with my values.'

choices.label: Do a mock interview with a friend or family member
choices.effect: Real practice! Your friend asks tough questions and gives honest feedback. You discover you say 'um' too much and fix it.

events.description: Interview day! First question: 'Tell me about a time you had to handle a difficult situation.' You're nervous and your mind goes blank for a moment. What do you do?

choices.label: Take a breath and say 'Great question, let me think for a moment'
choices.effect: Totally professional! Pausing to think shows confidence, not weakness. Your answer is better because you took a moment.

choices.label: Use the STAR method: Situation, Task, Action, Result
choices.effect: Structured storytelling! 'At my volunteer job (Situation), we needed to reorganize (Task), I created a schedule (Action), and we finished early (Result).' Clear and impressive!

choices.label: Be honest: 'I'm a bit nervous but I'm excited about this opportunity'
choices.effect: Authenticity! The interviewer smiles — they appreciate honesty. It actually relaxes the conversation and you answer naturally.

events.description: Curveball question: 'If you could have any superpower, what would it be and why?' This isn't about the answer — it's about how you think on your feet.

choices.label: Connect it to the job: 'Time control — I'd never miss a deadline!'
choices.effect: Clever tie-in! You showed creativity and job relevance in one answer. The interviewer laughs and nods.

choices.label: Be genuine: 'Teleportation — I value experiences and seeing the world'
choices.effect: Authentic answer that reveals your values! The interviewer sees you as thoughtful and genuine. There's no wrong answer here.

choices.label: Light humor: 'Mind reading — but only during interviews!'
choices.effect: Humor that acknowledges the situation! The interviewer laughs. A moment of levity makes the interview feel more like a conversation.

events.description: Interview is over! The interviewer asks 'Do you have any questions for us?' This is your chance to show interest and gather information.

choices.label: 'What does growth look like in this role?'
choices.effect: Shows ambition and long-term thinking! The interviewer appreciates someone who thinks beyond just getting hired.

choices.label: 'What do you enjoy most about working here?'
choices.effect: Flips the interview! Now THEY'RE sharing, and you get genuine insight into the workplace culture.

choices.label: 'What are the next steps in the hiring process?'
choices.effect: Practical and confident! You know exactly what to expect next and when to follow up.

events.description: After the interview: follow-up. You should send a thank-you note within 24 hours. What do you write?

choices.label: Reference a specific conversation point from the interview
choices.effect: Personalized! 'I especially enjoyed hearing about your volunteer program' shows you were listening and engaged.

choices.label: Briefly restate why you're a great fit for the role
choices.effect: Reinforcement! One more reminder of your strengths keeps you top-of-mind during their decision.

choices.label: Keep it brief: thank them, express enthusiasm, sign off
choices.effect: Concise professionalism! Busy hiring managers appreciate brevity. Two sentences and a polite close.

recap_template: You prepared for, aced, and followed up on a job interview! You practiced common questions, handled curveballs, asked smart questions, and sent a professional follow-up. These skills apply to every interview in your future.
positive_framing_rules: Never say the student bombed or failed a question
Frame nervousness as normal and manageable

title: Negotiation Sim
learning_objectives: Prepare for a negotiation with clear goals
Know when to compromise and when to hold firm

choices.label: Ask your boss for a raise at your part-time job
choices.effect: Raise negotiation! You've worked here 6 months, always on time, and took on extra responsibilities. Your current rate is $12/hour, similar jobs pay $14-15.

choices.label: Negotiate a deadline extension with your teacher
choices.effect: Academic negotiation! Your big project overlaps with two other deadlines. You need 3 extra days. The teacher values responsibility and communication.

choices.label: Negotiate with your team about project direction
choices.effect: Team negotiation! You want to go one direction, two teammates want another. You need consensus to move forward.

events.description: Preparation is 90% of negotiation. Before you walk in, you need to know: your goal, your best alternative if they say no (BATNA), and what the other side cares about. What do you prepare first?

choices.label: Research: what's the market rate / typical policy / team history?
choices.effect: Data is power! You found comparable rates/precedents that support your position. Facts are more persuasive than feelings.

choices.label: Think about what the other side wants and fears
choices.effect: Empathy as strategy! Your boss wants to keep good employees, your teacher wants to be fair, your team wants a good project. Understanding their goals helps you propose win-wins.

choices.label: Figure out your BATNA — what happens if they say no?
choices.effect: BATNA = Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement. Knowing your fallback gives you confidence and a clear walk-away point.

events.description: You're in the negotiation. You've made your case with evidence. The other party says 'I hear you, but I can only offer about half of what you're asking.' How do you respond?

choices.label: Counter with a specific number between your ask and their offer
choices.effect: Meeting in the middle shows flexibility! A specific counter (not 'maybe' or 'I guess') demonstrates you know your worth.

choices.label: Ask 'What's driving that limit?' — understand their constraints
choices.effect: Understanding their 'why' opens new solutions! Maybe there's a budget cycle, policy, or timeline you can work with.

choices.label: Propose non-monetary value: flexible schedule, title change, future review
choices.effect: Expanding the pie! When they can't give dollars, maybe they can give other things you value. Creative negotiation!

events.description: The negotiation is wrapping up. You didn't get everything you wanted, but you got more than the initial offer. How do you close?

choices.label: Summarize the agreement clearly: 'So we've agreed to X, Y, Z?'
choices.effect: Clear summary prevents misunderstandings! Both parties confirm the same terms. Put it in writing if possible.

choices.label: Set a date to revisit: 'Can we check in on this in 3 months?'
choices.effect: Built-in follow-up! This negotiation isn't the last one. A future check-in keeps the door open for more.

choices.label: Thank them for their time and flexibility
choices.effect: Ending with gratitude preserves the relationship! Negotiations are between people, not positions. You'll work with this person again.

events.description: Reflection: What did you learn about negotiation?

choices.label: Preparation made the biggest difference
choices.effect: Absolutely! Knowing your facts, their perspective, and your BATNA meant you were never caught off guard.

choices.label: The relationship matters as much as the outcome
choices.effect: Win-win > win-lose! A good negotiation strengthens the relationship. A scorched-earth win often costs more long-term.

choices.label: It gets easier with practice — this was a good start
choices.effect: Negotiation is a muscle! Every conversation where you advocate for yourself builds the skill. This was great practice.

recap_template: You practiced negotiation from preparation through closing! You learned about BATNA, evidence-based persuasion, creative solutions, and relationship-preserving communication. These skills serve you in career, relationships, and daily life.
positive_framing_rules: Never frame negotiation as adversarial or aggressive
Celebrate compromise as a sign of skill, not weakness
Frame all outcomes as learning experiences
ai_variation_allowed: Add different cultural contexts for negotiation
